nodes.name: NFCP electrodeposition
nodes.procedure: First, 1×1.2 cm² NF was cleaned by acetone, hydrochloric acid, anhydrous ethanol, and DI water, respectively, to remove the oxide layer of the NF surface. The electrolyte solutions containing 0.2 M CoCl₂·6H₂O, 0.05 M FeSO₄, 0.2 M NiCl₂·6H₂O, 0.5 M NaH₂PO₂, and 0.25 M NH₄Cl were formed, which were used in the electrodeposition process. In the chronoamperometry, a high frequency pulse current of 1 Hz and a current density of 60 mA·cm⁻² were introduced, and 1×1 cm² deposition occurs at 60°C with 20 min, marked as NFCP. The deposited electrode was rinsed several times with DI water and dried for 4 h in a vacuum atmosphere at 40°C.

nodes.name: RuO2/NF preparation
nodes.procedure: 40 mg RuO₂, 60 μL Nafion, and 200 μL ethanol were mixed and sonicated for more than 1 h to obtain uniform RuO₂ ink. Subsequently, the ink was dripped onto a clean NF surface and dried in a vacuum atmosphere of 60°C for 4 h.

nodes.description: OER performance comparison of multiple catalysts in alkaline simulated seawater
nodes.source_text: Electrocatalytic OER performance of NFCP, CNFCP, NFC, RuO2/NF, and NF was first investigated in alkaline simulated seawater (1.0 M KOH + 1.0 M NaCl) with the typical three electrode configuration... nodes.characterization_summary: NFCP, CNFCP, and NFC precursors show amorphous phase structure due to pulsed current and P; CNFCP shows diffraction peaks at 18.2° and 45.5° corresponding to NiFe2O4 and NiFe.
nodes.evidence_snippet: First, the surface structure and substance of the NFCP, CNFCP, and NFC precursor were characterized by XRD to evaluate the surface crystal phase composition, as shown in Figure S1.

nodes.characterization_summary: NFCP precursor shows spherical structures uniformly distributed on NF skeleton; activated NFCP shows nanosheet-like LDH structures with increased surface roughness.
nodes.evidence_snippet: SEM (scanning electron microscopy) and TEM (transmission electron microscopy) were used to characterize the morphology of the catalyst surface. The NFCP surface structure and activated catalyst are shown in Figure 1a-f.

nodes.characterization_summary: Activated NFCP exhibits distinct nanosheet structure with LDH (2.189 Å) and oxidized Ni(OH)2 (2.625 Å) lattice fringes confirmed by HRTEM and SEAD.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The activated NFCP exhibits a distinct nanosheet structure in TEM images as in Figure 1e-h and exhibits distinct LDH (2.189 Å) and oxidized Ni(OH)2 (2.625 Å) lattice under high magnification TEM and selected area electron diffraction (SEAD).

nodes.characterization_summary: NFCP shows uniform distribution of Ni, Fe, Co, and P elements on catalyst surface with atomic proportion 58.22:3.93:34.46:3.39.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The distribution of the deposited elements on the NFCP surface is shown in Figure 1i. Under the pulsed current, Ni, Fe, Co, and P are uniformly distributed on the catalyst surface.

nodes.characterization_summary: NFCP shows Ni 2p peaks at 852.7/870.3 eV (Ni-NiP), 853.69/871.59 eV (Ni-O); Co 2p at 778/793.7 eV (CoP), 779.8/795.1 eV (Co-O); Fe 2p at 706.3/718.9 eV (FeP), 710.5/721.4 eV (Fe-O); P 2p at 130.44/131.33 eV (metal-P).
nodes.evidence_snippet: X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was used to investigate the surface valence states and electronic structures of the NFCP, CNFCP, and NFC, as shown in Figure 2a-e.

nodes.characterization_summary: Activated NFCP shows Raman peaks at 457 cm⁻¹ (Eg) and 542 cm⁻¹ (Alg) attributed to NiFeCo(OH); NFC shows CoOOH and FeOOH peaks indicating phase separation; only Ni, Fe, Co signals after P leaching.
nodes.evidence_snippet: After reconstruction, the Raman spectral was employed, and two peaks were found at Eg and Alg in 457 and 542 cm⁻¹, attributed to NiFeCo(OH). Characteristic peaks belonging to CoOOH and FeOOH were detected on the NFC surface.

nodes.characterization_summary: NFCP shows Fe leaching rate of 32.3% after 1h OER and >60% after 50h; Co leaching 10% after 1h and 50% after 50h during surface reconstruction and OER stages.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Considering the corrosion caused by chlorine adsorption, we also investigated the metal content of NFCP in simulated seawater through ICP-OES (inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer), as shown in Figure 4e.
